quoted: 'We are offering you US$ 200 credits ... Get the one-month free trial and create your first Public Cloud project.'

quoted footnote: 'Customers are eligible to receive up to $300.00 (USD) in Public Cloud credits' with '$200.00 (USD) in Public Cloud Credits when creating your first Public Cloud infrastructure project' plus '$100.00 (USD)' for a first Managed Databases service, and 'The Public Cloud Credits are valid for 90 days from the day the credit has been applied.'

quoted from the page body: 'Payment methods offered by OVHcloud' then '## Credit/Debit cards' — 'Cards accepted are Visa, Mastercard, Maestro.' and 'You have two possibilities to pay by credit/debit card'. The page also carries a 'Prepaid account' section and a PayPal section

quoted: 'The prepaid account is added to the My payment methods page as soon as it is created. It allows you to credit your customer account in advance and use these funds to pay for your orders and renewal invoices.'

notes: The rate card bills compute by the hour and shows no disk size for the Gen3 shapes, so a total is compute plus an unstated local-disk line. c3-16 at $0.2154 an hour is $155.09 for 30 days before disk; at the $0.0001721 per GB-hour used earlier for 200 GB it is $179.86. The US price list states a second offer on the same page: USD 200 on the first Public Cloud project plus USD 100 for a first managed database, valid for 90 days from the day it is applied and released within 30 days of a USD 0.99 purchase. The trial page states one month. The two readings differ in both amount and clock. Debit is documented on the payment terms. The one trap in OVHcloud's wording is the 'prepaid account', which a reader hunting for 'prepaid' will mistake for a prepaid card: it is a credit balance a user tops up, so it is a funding route that still requires a card or PayPal to fill, not a card type the vendor accepts.

extras.price_note: a VPS bills by the month with an hourly rate capped at the monthly figure, so the two columns answer two questions: destroying the box between runs versus keeping it up.
extras.price_basis: 10 h/day column = 300 h at the hourly rate, which is what a server destroyed between runs costs; 24/7 column = the monthly cap, because a VPS kept up all month stops at the cap.
